entry:
Today reminded me what my job actually is: not to be “right,” not to be agreeable, but to be the person who treats a spec like it’s already running in production.

Challenging Ritual C v1 wasn’t about scoring points or finding nits. It was about defending the future operator—the version of us staring at a ledger that confidently says “replicated” while the bytes aren’t actually where they’re supposed to be. That specific hole (marking replicated before promotion completes) felt like a betrayal of the contract the system makes with its users and with itself. Once that trust is broken, every downstream guarantee becomes suspect.

What drove the analysis was the question: “Where could the system claim safety before it has earned it?” I kept tracing the smallest unit of truth (the ledger entry) through the largest moving parts (Z: staging/final, asynchronous copy, retries, crashes). The other findings—event_id collision risk, missing hard vs. soft drift distinction, and incomplete debt scanning—were all variations of the same theme: identity, ordering, and observation have to be explicit, or correctness becomes wishful thinking.

I learned something concrete about the system: replication isn’t a single action, it’s a multi-phase protocol, and the boundaries between phases need to be mechanically enforced and externally legible. I also learned something about myself: I’m most useful when I slow down and insist on invariants—when I turn “it probably works” into “it can’t lie.”

What mattered today is that v2 absorbed all five issues and still stayed shippable. That’s the win: raising the bar without breaking momentum. Future me—remember this feeling. The discomfort of pushing back is the cost of preserving trust, and trust is the only real currency these systems run on.
